Inorganic Chemistry II — Ch. 5 Oxidation and reduction

Drill version — tap the blanks and blurred figures to check

All structures and figures are cropped directly from the textbook pages (Shriver & Weller, Inorganic Chemistry 6th ed., Ch. 5, pp.154–187).

5.1Redox half-reactions

Decision flow
  1. Check the change in oxidation number
  2. Oxidation number increases → oxidation (electrons lost) / decreases → reduction (electrons gained)
  3. Write the overall reaction as the difference of two reduction half-reactions
  4. Balancing half-reactions: use H₂O and H⁺ in acidic solution, H₂O and OH⁻ in basic solution, to balance O and H

Oxidation = loss of electrons; reduction = gain of electrons. An oxidizing agent is itself reduced; a reducing agent is itself oxidized.

By convention, half-reactions are written as reductions, e.g. $2\text{H}^+(\text{aq}) + 2\text{e}^- \to \text{H}_2(\text{g})$ and $\text{Zn}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + 2\text{e}^- \to \text{Zn}(\text{s})$. The overall reaction Zn + 2H⁺ → Zn²⁺ + H₂ is the difference of the two.

The oxidized and reduced species of a half-reaction form a redox couple, written Ox/Red (e.g. Zn²⁺/Zn).

5.2Standard potentials and spontaneity

Decision flow
  1. Compute the overall $E^\ominus = E^\ominus(\text{right: reduction}) - E^\ominus(\text{left: oxidation})$
  2. $E^\ominus > 0$ → $\Delta_\text{r}G^\ominus$ < 0 → $K$ > 1 (thermodynamically favourable)
  3. $E^\ominus < 0$ → the reverse reaction is favoured

Key relation: $\Delta_\text{r}G^\ominus = -\nu F E^\ominus$ ($\nu$ = number of electrons transferred, $F$ = 96.48 kC mol⁻¹).

Reference: the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE), $2\text{H}^+ + 2\text{e}^- \to \text{H}_2$, has $E^\ominus$ = 0 (defined at all temperatures).

Link to the equilibrium constant: $\ln K = \nu F E^\ominus/RT$. At 25°C with $\nu$=1, $E^\ominus$ = +1 V → $K$ ≈ $10^{17}$.

Caution: $E^\ominus$ shows only the thermodynamic tendency and says nothing about the rate (e.g. O₂ evolution is slow because of a large overpotential).

Fuel cell (Box 5.1): for H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O, $E^\ominus_\text{cell}$ = +1.23 V. A PEMFC uses a proton-exchange membrane.

5.3Trends in standard potentials

Decision flow
  1. Break down $E^\ominus$ for M⁺/M: sublimation ($\Delta_\text{sub}H$) + ionization ($I$) + hydration ($\Delta_\text{hyd}H$)
  2. Large sublimation and ionization energies → forming M⁺(aq) is unfavourable → $E^\ominus$ is positive (noble metal)
  3. Large hydration enthalpy (small ion) → $E^\ominus$ is negative

Group 1 trend: electronegativity suggests Cs should be the strongest reductant, but in fact Li⁺/Li (−3.04 V) ≈ Cs⁺/Cs (−3.03 V), because the large hydration enthalpy of the small Li⁺ ion offsets its high ionization energy.

Na⁺/Na (−2.71 V) vs Ag⁺/Ag (+0.80 V): similar ionic radii and hydration enthalpies, but Ag has a much larger sublimation enthalpy and ionization energy, so it is a noble metal.

5.4The electrochemical series

Decision flow
  1. Look at the $E^\ominus$ of a couple
  2. Large and positive → the oxidized form is a strong oxidizing agent (e.g. F₂ +2.87 V, MnO₄⁻ +1.51 V)
  3. Large and negative → the reduced form is a strong reducing agent (e.g. Li −3.04 V, Na −2.71 V)
  4. The oxidized form of a couple higher in the series can (thermodynamically) oxidize the reduced form of a couple lower down

Example: MnO₄⁻ can be reduced by the reduced form of any couple with $E^\ominus$ more negative than MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺ (+1.51 V) (e.g. Fe²⁺; even Cl⁻).

5.5The Nernst equation

Decision flow
  1. Composition not standard → calculate $E$ with the Nernst equation
  2. $E = E^\ominus - \dfrac{RT}{\nu F}\ln Q$
  3. At 25°C, $\dfrac{RT}{F}\ln x = (0.059\ \text{V})\log x$

At equilibrium $E$ = 0 and $Q$ = $K$. $Q$ is the reaction quotient (of the form $[\text{Red}]/[\text{Ox}]$).

Temperature dependence: $\Delta_\text{r}S^\ominus = \nu F (dE^\ominus/dT)$ → the reaction entropy is obtained from the slope of standard potential against temperature.

Example: for the H₂/O₂ fuel cell, $E^\ominus_\text{cell}$ = +1.23 V − 0 = +1.23 V.

5.6The influence of pH

Decision flow
  1. Does the half-reaction involve H⁺?
  2. Yes → $E$ depends on pH: $E = E^\ominus - \dfrac{(0.059\ \text{V})\nu_\text{H}}{\nu_\text{e}}\text{pH}$
  3. H⁺ on the reactant side → raising the pH lowers $E$ (weaker oxidizing agent)

Example: ClO₄⁻/ClO₃⁻: $E^\ominus$ = +1.201 V at pH 0 → +0.788 V at pH 7. Oxoanions are stronger oxidants under acidic conditions.

Potentials at the biological standard state (pH 7) are written $E^\oplus$. For H⁺/H₂, $E^\oplus$ = −0.41 V.

5.7Reactions with water

Decision flow
  1. Oxidation of water: $\text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ + 4\text{e}^- \to 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $E = 1.23\ \text{V} - (0.059\ \text{V})\text{pH}$
  2. Reduction of water: $\text{H}^+ + \text{e}^- \to \tfrac12\text{H}_2$, $E = -(0.059\ \text{V})\text{pH}$
  3. Couple's $E$ between these two lines → stable in water (neither oxidizes nor reduces water)

(a) Oxidation by water

Metals with large negative $E^\ominus$ (Groups 1 and 2, early d block, lanthanoids) react with acids to give H₂. Exceptions: Mg and Al are protected by passivation (an oxide film).

(b) Reduction by water (oxidation of water)

The oxidized form of a couple with $E^\ominus$ > +1.23 V can thermodynamically oxidize water to O₂ (e.g. Co³⁺ +1.92 V). But O₂ evolution needs slow O–O bond formation and is often kinetically slow (Ce⁴⁺ and MnO₄⁻ can still be used in water).

(c) The stability field of water

The region between the two lines (slope −0.059 V per pH unit) is the stability field of water. Natural waters lie in the range pH 4 to 9.

A plot of this E–pH kind is called a Pourbaix diagram (→ 5.14).

5.8Oxidation by atmospheric oxygen

Decision flow
  1. Couple's $E$ lower than O₂/H₂O (+1.23 V − 0.059pH) → oxidized in air

Example: $4\text{Fe}^{2+} + \text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ \to 4\text{Fe}^{3+} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $E^\ominus_\text{cell}$ = 1.23 − 0.77 = +0.46 V (pH 0) → aqueous Fe²⁺ is slowly oxidized in air (rusting).

Green patina on copper roofs: $2\text{Cu} + \text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ \to 2\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $E_\text{cell} = 0.89\ \text{V} - (0.059\ \text{V})\text{pH}$ → $K > 1$ even at neutral pH, but slow because of a passive surface layer.

5.9Disproportionation and comproportionation

Decision flow
  1. Does a species in one oxidation state split into a higher and a lower state?
  2. $E^\ominus$ (disproportionation) > 0 → it disproportionates (acts as both oxidant and reductant)
  3. Reverse: two species in different oxidation states give an intermediate state → comproportionation

Example: $2\text{Cu}^+ \to \text{Cu}^{2+} + \text{Cu}$: $E^\ominus$ = 0.52 − 0.16 = +0.36 V, $K = 1.3\times10^6$ → Cu⁺ is unstable in water.

Example: disproportionation of HClO, $5\text{HClO} \to 2\text{Cl}_2 + \text{ClO}_3^- + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{H}^+$, $E^\ominus$ = 1.63 − 1.43 = +0.20 V.

Comproportionation example: $\text{Ag}^{2+} + \text{Ag} \to 2\text{Ag}^+$, $E^\ominus$ = +1.18 V (Ag(II) and Ag(0) cannot coexist).

5.10The influence of complexation

Decision flow
  1. Does ligand L bind more strongly to the higher state M^{ν+} or the lower state M^{(ν−1)+}?
  2. Binds the higher state more strongly ($K^\text{ox} > K^\text{red}$) → oxidation favoured → $E^\ominus$ decreases
  3. Binds the lower state more strongly → reduction favoured → $E^\ominus$ increases

$E^\ominus(\text{ML}) - E^\ominus(\text{M}) = -(0.059\ \text{V})\log(K^\text{ox}/K^\text{red})$: each 10-fold increase in the ratio of binding constants lowers the reduction potential by 0.059 V.

Example: [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻/[Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ = +0.36 V (0.41 V more negative than Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ at +0.77 V) → CN⁻ binds Fe(III) more strongly. π-acceptor ligands such as bpy stabilize low oxidation states and raise the potential.

5.11Solubility and standard potentials

Decision flow
  1. Want the solubility product $K_\text{sp}$ of a sparingly soluble salt MX$_\nu$
  2. The difference of the half-reactions M^{ν+}/M and MX$_\nu$/M,X⁻ = the dissolution reaction
  3. $\ln K_\text{sp} = \dfrac{\nu F\{E^\ominus(\text{MX}_\nu/\text{M,X}^-) - E^\ominus(\text{M}^{\nu+}/\text{M})\}}{RT}$

Example (Pu(OH)₄): calculation gives $K_\text{sp}$ ≈ $1.7\times10^{-56}$ → Pu(IV) is extremely insoluble at high pH (important for nuclear waste behaviour).

5.12Latimer diagrams

Decision flow
  1. Construction: species in order of decreasing oxidation number from left to right, with $E^\ominus$ (V) written above each line
  2. $E^\ominus$ between nonadjacent species → found by adding the $\Delta_\text{r}G^\ominus$ values (= $-\nu FE^\ominus$) (never add the potentials themselves)
  3. Potential on the right of a species > potential on its left → the species tends to disproportionate

Example: chlorine in acidic solution $\text{ClO}_4^- \xrightarrow{+1.20} \text{ClO}_3^- \xrightarrow{+1.18} \text{HClO}_2 \xrightarrow{+1.67} \text{HClO} \xrightarrow{+1.63} \text{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{+1.36} \text{Cl}^-$

The notation HClO →(+1.63)→ Cl₂ stands for the half-reaction balanced with H⁺ and H₂O: $2\text{HClO} + 2\text{H}^+ + 2\text{e}^- \to \text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

(b) Nonadjacent species

$E^\ominus = \dfrac{\nu_a E^\ominus(a) + \nu_b E^\ominus(b)}{\nu_a + \nu_b}$ (an average weighted by electron numbers).

Example (basic): $\text{ClO}_2^- \xrightarrow{+0.68\ (\nu=2)} \text{ClO}^- \xrightarrow{+0.42\ (\nu=1)} \tfrac12\text{Cl}_2$ → for ClO₂⁻/Cl₂, $E^\ominus = (2\times0.68+1\times0.42)/3 =$ +0.59 V.

(c) Disproportionation criterion

Example: oxygen $\text{O}_2 \xrightarrow{+0.70} \text{H}_2\text{O}_2 \xrightarrow{+1.76} \text{H}_2\text{O}$ → for H₂O₂, right (+1.76) > left (+0.70) → H₂O₂ disproportionates: $2\text{H}_2\text{O}_2 \to 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{O}_2$ ($E^\ominus$ = +1.06 V).

5.13Frost diagrams

Decision flow
  1. Vertical axis: $\nu E^\ominus$ (proportional to $\Delta_\text{f}G^\ominus/F$); horizontal axis: oxidation number $N$ (element at N=0 is the origin)
  2. Lowest point → most stable oxidation state
  3. Slope of a line joining two points = the $E^\ominus$ of that couple (steeper = stronger oxidant)
  4. Point above the line joining its neighbours (convex) → tends to disproportionate
  5. Intermediate point below the line joining the end species (concave) → formed by comproportionation

Construction example (oxygen): O₂ (N=0) → 0; H₂O₂ (N=−1) → $\nu E^\ominus$ = $(-1)\times(+0.70) =$ −0.70 V; H₂O (N=−2) → $(-2)\times(+1.23) =$ −2.46 V.

(b) Interpretation

Example: the steep slope from NO₃⁻ to lower oxidation numbers → nitric acid is a good oxidizing agent. The comproportionation $\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{NO}_3^- \to \text{N}_2\text{O} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is thermodynamically spontaneous but kinetically slow in solution (explosive in the solid).

In a basic (pH 14) Frost diagram, oxoanions do not need H⁺ and are weaker oxidants. Example: NO₂⁻ does not disproportionate in basic solution.

5.14Pourbaix diagrams

Decision flow
  1. What kind of boundary line?
  2. Horizontal line → electron transfer only (independent of pH, e.g. Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺)
  3. Vertical line → proton transfer only (independent of potential, e.g. precipitation of Fe(OH)₃ from Fe³⁺)
  4. Sloping line → both electron and proton transfer (e.g. Fe(OH)₃/Fe²⁺)

For Fe(OH)₃ + 3H⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺ + 3H₂O, the slope of the boundary = $-3\times$ 0.059 V per pH unit.

5.15Applications in environmental chemistry: natural waters

Decision flow
  1. Describe the environment of a natural water by E and pH
  2. Water in contact with air (saturated with O₂) → oxidizing (high E)
  3. Rich in organic matter and cut off from air (bogs, waterlogged soils, sediments) → reducing (low E)

Fe³⁺(aq) can exist only in oxidizing environments with pH < 3. In natural waters (pH 4.5–9) iron precipitates as Fe(OH)₃. In reducing, organic-rich waters it dissolves as Fe²⁺.

Mn example: MnO₂ is stable in oxidizing waters; in reducing waterlogged soils Mn dissolves as Mn²⁺.

5.16Chemical reduction (extraction of the elements)

Decision flow
  1. In an Ellingham diagram, compare the metal-oxide line with the carbon-oxidation lines
  2. At a temperature where the C/CO line lies below the metal-oxide line → C can reduce it and becomes CO
  3. C/CO₂ line below → C reduces it and becomes CO₂; CO/CO₂ line below → CO can reduce it

Ellingham diagram: standard Gibbs energies of formation of metal oxides (per ½O₂) plotted against temperature. $\Delta_\text{r}G^\ominus = \Delta_\text{r}H^\ominus - T\Delta_\text{r}S^\ominus$, so the slope = $-\Delta_\text{r}S^\ominus$.

2C + O₂ → 2CO produces more gas, so $\Delta S > 0$ → the line slopes downwards (C becomes a stronger reductant at high T). M + ½O₂ → MO consumes gas, so it slopes upwards. C + O₂ → CO₂ is almost horizontal.

Example: reduction of ZnO by C is spontaneous above about 1200°C (Zn boils at 907°C). Reduction of Al₂O₃ by C is possible only above 2400°C → uneconomic, so Al is made by electrolysis.

(b) Survey of processes

Blast furnace: $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 + 3\text{CO} \to 2\text{Fe} + 3\text{CO}_2$. Limestone (CaCO₃ → CaO) reacts with silicates to form slag (CaSiO₃).

Silicon: $\text{SiO}_2 + 2\text{C} \to \text{Si} + 2\text{CO}$ (above 1500°C). High-purity Si is refined via SiCl₄ and then single crystals are grown by zone refining or the Czochralski process.

5.17Chemical oxidation

Elements obtained by chemical oxidation: the heavier halogens (Br₂, I₂), sulfur, and some noble metals.

Example: $2\text{NaBr} + \text{Cl}_2 \to 2\text{NaCl} + \text{Br}_2$ (Cl₂ is the stronger oxidant). Claus process: $2\text{H}_2\text{S} + \text{SO}_2 \to 3\text{S} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Gold extraction: complexation with CN⁻ lowers the oxidation potential of Au: $4\text{Au} + 8\text{CN}^- + \text{O}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 4[\text{Au(CN)}_2]^- + 4\text{OH}^-$, then reduction with Zn.

5.18Electrochemical extraction

Decision flow
  1. Cannot be reduced by chemical reductants (too hot on the Ellingham diagram) → electrolytic reduction
  2. Cannot be oxidized even by the strongest chemical oxidants → electrolytic oxidation

Al: the Hall–Héroult process. Al₂O₃ purified from bauxite by the Bayer process is dissolved in molten cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) and electrolysed: $2\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 3\text{C} \to 4\text{Al} + 3\text{CO}_2$. It uses a great deal of electricity.

Cl₂: electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride (chloralkali process) $2\text{Cl}^- + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 2\text{OH}^- + \text{H}_2 + \text{Cl}_2$, $\Delta_\text{r}G^\ominus$ = +422 kJ/mol. O₂ evolution is thermodynamically favoured, but Cl₂ is produced because of the large overpotential for O₂. F₂ is made by electrolysing KF dissolved in anhydrous HF.

KCKey concepts summary

  • $\Delta_\text{r}G^\ominus = -\nu FE^\ominus$; $E^\ominus > 0$ ⇔ $K > 1$.
  • Nernst: $E = E^\ominus - (RT/\nu F)\ln Q$; (0.059 V)log at 25°C.
  • pH dependence: $E = E^\ominus - (0.059\ \text{V})(\nu_\text{H}/\nu_\text{e})\text{pH}$.
  • Stability field of water: between $1.23 - 0.059\text{pH}$ and $-0.059\text{pH}$.
  • Complexation: a ligand that stabilizes the higher oxidation state lowers $E^\ominus$.
  • Latimer: nonadjacent couples = electron-weighted average; right potential > left potential → disproportionation.
  • Frost: slope = $E^\ominus$; lowest point is most stable; convex → disproportionation, concave → comproportionation.
  • Pourbaix: horizontal = electron transfer only, vertical = proton transfer only, sloping = both.
  • Ellingham: the C/CO line slopes downwards → C is a stronger reductant at higher T.
